bullets: ‘The cold within him froze his old features, nipped his pointed nose, shrivelled his cheek’: physical cold reflects emotional coldness.
‘External heat and cold had little influence on Scrooge. No warmth could warm, no wintry weather chill him.’: he is colder than the weather.
‘He carried his own low temperature always about with him’.
Bob’s ‘one coal’: Scrooge spreads cold to others.
Foggy, dark streets; Scrooge’s gloomy rooms; ‘darkness is cheap, and Scrooge liked it’.
‘solitary as an oyster’; he likes to ‘edge his way along the crowded paths of life, warning all human sympathy to keep its distance’.
Fred ‘all in a glow’; warm, ruddy, sparkling.
Fezziwig’s ball: the fire, food, dancing: ‘snug, and warm, and dry, and bright’.
Ghost of Christmas Present: a blazing fire, a feast, a torch.
Cratchits: the fire, the pudding ‘blazing in half of half-a-quartern of ignited brandy’.
Stave 5: ‘Make up the fires’: Scrooge spreads warmth to Bob.
Stave 4: Scrooge’s death goes unmourned; his body lies alone: ‘plundered and bereft, unwatched, unwept, uncared for’.
Isolation is self-chosen and self-punishing (Fred: ‘Who suffers by his ill whims? Himself, always.’).

callouts.p: Dickens uses cold and warmth as a moral thermometer: coldness signals isolation and selfishness, while warmth signals community and generosity, so Scrooge’s journey is literally from cold to warm.

model: Context: Dickens’s childhood loneliness; middle-class indifference
exam.q: Explain how Dickens presents isolation elsewhere in the novella. (20 marks)
exam.tip: Track the motif from cold to warm.

mistakes.r: Link cold and warmth to character, morality and isolation.

quotes.a: Coldness is part of his nature.

summary: Isolation, warmth and cold form a symbolic pattern: Scrooge’s coldness and isolation in Stave 1 give way to warmth, fire and company in Stave 5, so temperature tracks his moral state and his relationship with others.
